anomaly_def.Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Persisted heap and index pages contain physical or logical corruptions that render on-disk structures internally inconsistent with the logical data model.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage subsystem cannot deliver the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required by the database engine, causing sustained I/O queuing and stalls.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space on data, log, temp, or backup volumes falls to or below hard limits, preventing successful allocation, extension, or recycling operations.

When these three conditions coexist, the database may exhibit a tangled symptom set: index and table scans intermittently miss or duplicate rows; integrity-check utilities report checksum or key-order errors; meanwhile foreground sessions and background tasks accrue extreme I/O wait times, and log flush, buffer-I/O, and allocation waits dominate wait profiles. Space-related allocation failures, auto-extend errors, or frozen transaction logs further stall change processing and exacerbate I/O queue depths. Checkpoint and recovery operations lengthen, and corruption-detection mechanisms may be delayed or starved, causing sudden bursts of corruption errors when space is finally freed or I/O resumes. Administrators may observe a cascade: first space alerts, then throughput saturation, followed by corruption reports, making the root causes appear intertwined and difficult to isolate.

Causally, sustained I/O saturation slows down page writes and checkpoints, increasing the window in which torn, partially written, or out-of-order pages can arise—heightening the likelihood of data-block and index corruption, especially after forced restarts. Simultaneously, dwindling storage space limits the ability of the engine to allocate new pages, perform online rebuilds, or write full redo and archive logs, forcing aggressive reuse of existing space. This pressure can interrupt in-flight I/O, amplify fragmentation, and impede verification or repair utilities that themselves require both throughput and space. The resulting feedback loop—corruption that demands I/O to repair, throttled I/O that cannot keep up, and no free space to reallocate or rebuild—drives the database into an increasingly unstable and performance-degraded state.

entry.official_description: ALTER TABLE causes auto_increment resequencing, resulting in duplicate entry '%-.192s' for key '%-.192s'
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with logical data inconsistency, structural corruption, uniqueness conflicts, or referential-integrity rules being violated by the workload or storage state.
entry.solution_guidance: Validate data consistency, inspect constraints and index integrity, and check whether data-cleaning, repair, or workload correction is required before retrying.
